title: Local Euclidean spaces
body:
A manifold gives us a way to do calculus on a space without first flattening the whole space into one Euclidean map. We work locally, using enough coordinate labels to differentiate functions and describe motion. Smooth conversions between overlapping descriptions then let those calculations fit together.
For the soil scientists' two-dimensional terrain, the points are actual ground locations. A rigid board supplies nearby labels, but its distances need not equal distances measured on the curved ground. Temperature readings and probe routes belong to the surface, whichever scientist records them.
General relativity uses the same idea for four-dimensional spacetime. A metric is additional structure specifying what clocks and rulers measure. So having local coordinates does not, by itself, supply a measuring rule or declare the space physically flat.
statement: Local coordinates allow calculus without assuming a globally flat space.

title: Compatible local coordinate descriptions
statement: A smooth \(n\)-manifold has compatible local \(n\)-coordinate descriptions; a metric is extra structure.

title: Terrain survey: one surface
body:
Let \(M\) be the ground surface of a kame-and-kettle landscape. Each scientist labels a small patch by projecting its points onto a rigid board's grid. The patch must be small enough that the projection has a smooth inverse: given two board coordinates, the scientist can identify one ground point again.
The temperature \(T(p)\) and a measured curvature estimate \(K(p)\) are scalar readings attached to a point \(p\). Surface grass growth needs a direction and magnitude instead, so it is represented by a tangent vector. Two scientists can therefore give the same peg different coordinates while agreeing on its temperature and physical growth direction.
Their board grids may differ in scale, orientation and obliqueness. The overlap rules reconcile those numerical records into one surface description. Thus the manifold is the ground with its compatible local structure, rather than the collection of flat boards.
\explanation{dimension}{Why is this still two-dimensional?}{A location on the ground needs two independent local labels. Height in a surrounding three-dimensional picture is fixed once the surface location is chosen, so it does not add an independent direction of movement along the ground. Curvature changes geometry, not this local dimension.}
statement: Overlapping grids describe one two-dimensional ground surface, not separate flat pieces.

title: Coordinates as labels
body:
A coordinate chart assigns numerical labels to points in a local region of a manifold. Changing the chart changes those labels, rather than the underlying points.
It helps to distinguish a point \(p\) from its coordinate tuple \(x(p)\). The inverse map \(x^{-1}\) lets us go back from the tuple to the point, which is essential if a calculation with numbers is to identify a unique location.
In the terrain survey, a straight board grid supplies the labels through projection. Its axes need not be orthogonal or calibrated to ground distance. This freedom is why a chart is a labelling rule, while a metric supplies a separate measuring rule.
statement: Coordinates label points; they do not prescribe lengths or angles.

title: An invertible local labelling
statement: A chart \(x:U\to x(U)\subset\mathbb R^n\) gives a smooth, invertible local labelling.

title: Terrain survey: one board
body:
Each scientist works on a small region \(U\) and uses a straight grid on a rigid tangent board to define \(x:U\rightarrow\mathbb R^2\). Ground points are mapped smoothly and one-to-one onto the board, whose axes may be differently scaled and need not be perpendicular. The patch must be small enough that the projection and its inverse remain smooth and unambiguous.
With these two labels, the scientist can express temperature as a function and record the probe's track as \(x^1(t),x^2(t)\). They label the curved ground; they do not replace it with a flat surface. There is an important limitation to the board picture. The board is tangent at its reference point, rather than at every point of the curved patch. Coordinate basis vectors elsewhere follow the surface coordinate curves there, rather than the fixed arrows drawn on the board.
\explanation{overlap}{Why do different boards still describe one motion?}{On an overlap the scientists agree a smooth conversion \(y^i=y^i(x^1,x^2)\). Substituting the same track \(x^j(t)\) gives its new description \(y^i(t)\). The chain rule relates its coordinate rates:
\[\frac{dy^i}{dt}=\frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}\frac{dx^j}{dt}.\]
Here \(j=1,2\) is summed. Thus the coordinate rates change by the Jacobian, while the probe follows the same ground route. The relabelling itself moves no physical point.}
statement: A board projection supplies local labels while the measured ground stays curved.

title: Changing labels, not points
body:
A coordinate transformation changes a point's numerical labels while keeping the point fixed. If a peg is recorded as \(x(p)\) by one scientist and \(y(p)\) by another, the transition connects those two records; it does not move the peg.
A scalar measurement such as temperature stays the same, although the formula expressing it in the new labels usually changes. Vector components change too, because the coordinate basis changes. We must therefore distinguish the object from the numbers used to describe it.
In GR, this coordinate freedom is broader than the Lorentz transformations between SR inertial frames. Curved spacetime generally needs arbitrary smooth transitions between local charts, rather than one global linear frame change.
statement: A change of coordinates alters descriptions, not the underlying points or measurements.

title: The overlap transition
body:
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be overlapping \cref{charts}{math.coordinate_chart.definition}. For a point \(p\) in their common region, the transition map takes \(x(p)\) to \(y(p)\). First use \(x^{-1}\) to recover the point, then apply \(y\) to find its other labels. This composition, \(y\circ x^{-1}\), is smooth and has a smooth inverse on the overlap.
The notation \(y^i=y^i(x^1,\ldots,x^n)\) abbreviates this composition; the inverse gives \(x^i=x^i(y)\). Thus the transition acts between numerical descriptions, moving no physical point and changing no measured scalar value.
\explanation{scalar}{Does the temperature formula stay the same?}{The reading stays the same, but its formula usually changes. Write \(T_x=T\circ x^{-1}\) and \(T_y=T\circ y^{-1}\). Then
\[T_y(y(p))=T(p)=T_x(x(p)).\]
For example, replacing a metre label by a centimetre label changes the numerical argument of the formula. The physical reading is unchanged, but we must adjust the formula to accept the new numerical argument. This is why an invariant measurement need not have an identical coordinate expression.}
statement: The transition \(y\circ x^{-1}\) converts labels for the same point on an overlap.

title: Terrain survey: reconciling neighbours
statement: Straight board grids can give nonlinear transitions when they project different curved patches.

title: Jacobian of the change
body:
For overlapping charts \(x\) and \(y\), write the transition as \(y=y(x)\). To describe small coordinate changes near a point, collect the derivatives into the Jacobian \(J^i{}_j=\partial y^i/\partial x^j\). At each overlap point it is invertible. A nonlinear transition can have a Jacobian that varies with position.
Now let a smooth probe route cross that point. Because \(y\) depends on the probe's \(x\)-coordinates, the chain rule relates its two coordinate-rate descriptions:
\[\frac{dy^i}{dt}=J^i{}_j\frac{dx^j}{dt}.\]
Repeated \(j\) is summed over the coordinate directions. The Jacobian changes the component numbers to account for the new labels. It does not change the probe's motion.
\explanation{inverse}{Why is the Jacobian invertible?}{Converting from \(x\) to \(y\) and back must restore the original coordinates. Differentiating that identity with the chain rule gives:
\[\frac{\partial x^k}{\partial y^i}\frac{\partial y^i}{\partial x^j}=\delta^k{}_j.\]
The derivative matrices are inverses. A zero determinant would signal a failure of these coordinates, not automatically a physical singularity.}
This forward-and-inverse pair is also what makes the component changes of vectors and covectors fit together. Later tensor transformation rules use these same factors.
statement: The Jacobian converts infinitesimal coordinate changes; its inverse reverses the conversion.

title: Lorentz transformations as a special case
body:
The \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations} are special coordinate changes between standard inertial frames in flat spacetime. They obey additional physical and geometric restrictions, including preservation of the Minkowski metric.
A general coordinate transition need not be linear or global, and need not correspond to changing inertial observer. So Lorentz transformations belong within the broader language of coordinate changes, but do not exhaust that freedom.
statement: Lorentz transformations are a restricted class of spacetime coordinate changes.

title: Not a change of physics
body:
Changing coordinates changes our description, rather than the physical situation. A difficult grid can make a simple geometry look complicated, while a well-chosen grid can simplify its formulae.
This is useful freedom, but it does not move manifold points or change the underlying scalar measurements. When two coordinate expressions look different, first ask whether they describe the same objects using different labels.
statement: Relabelling a physical situation does not change it.

title: A history through spacetime
body:
A worldline follows a particle, observer, clock, detector or light signal through spacetime. Instead of listing isolated \cref{Spacetime events}{sr.spacetime_event}, we collect the successive events of that history into one curve.
It includes the time information as well as position. A particle that stays at one spatial location therefore still traces a worldline as time passes; its history is not just a stationary dot on a spatial map.
statement: A worldline records a history through spacetime, not just a spatial track.

title: A parametrised spacetime history
body:
A smooth worldline is a map \(\gamma:I\to M\) from a real parameter interval \(I\) into a spacetime \cref{manifold}{math.manifold} \(M\). In a chart its coordinate functions are \(x^\mu(\lambda)\). As \(\lambda\) varies, the map picks out successive events of the particle or signal. Thus the parameter labels positions along this particular history; it is not an additional spacetime dimension. When the history belongs to a massive clock, a useful parameter is \cref{Proper time}{sr.proper_time} \(\tau\); a light ray has no proper-time clock parameter of this kind.
\explanation{parameter}{Is the parameter another spacetime coordinate?}{No. It labels positions along this particular curve. The spacetime point \(\gamma(\lambda)\) already has its coordinate tuple. Two smooth, regularly invertible, increasing parameter choices can describe the same oriented path, while giving different numerical derivatives along it. Physical time or proper time, when supplied, gives the rate a particular meaning.}
statement: A worldline is a curve \(\gamma:I\to M\) through spacetime, labelled by a parameter.

title: Curve versus coordinate plot
body:
A curve \(\gamma\) specifies points of the manifold, whereas a \cref{chart}{math.coordinate_chart.definition} supplies their numerical labels. In that chart we see the coordinate functions \(x\circ\gamma\). Another chart supplies \(y\circ\gamma\), which may give a quite different-looking plot.
The plot is therefore one description of the curve, not the curve itself. A \cref{Minkowski diagram}{sr.minkowski_diagram} is a useful spacetime example of this distinction. Choosing more complicated coordinates can make a free particle's plotted history bend without introducing a physical force or acceleration.
statement: Different coordinate plots can represent exactly the same curve.

title: Terrain survey: the mobile probe
body:
The mobile probe follows a smooth route \(\gamma:t\mapsto\gamma(t)\in M\), with \(t\) in seconds. In one board chart its track is \((x^1(t),x^2(t))\). Across an overlap another scientist records \((y^1(t),y^2(t))\). The formulas change at the overlap, but both scientists are following the same ground points. Nothing makes the probe jump merely because another board supplies its labels.
\explanation{history}{Is the surface route itself a worldline?}{Strictly, the route on \(M\) is a spatial curve, not yet a spacetime worldline. Including time produces the spacetime history \(t\mapsto(t,\gamma(t))\). For example, a stationary probe has a constant surface position, but its time coordinate continues to change, so it still traces a spacetime history. The distinction keeps a two-dimensional ground map separate from spacetime.}
statement: A surface route becomes a spacetime history when time is included.

title: Tangent direction
body:
For a smooth spacetime curve \(\gamma(\lambda)\), choose a chart \(x^\mu\) near the event \(p=\gamma(\lambda_0)\). Differentiate its coordinate functions at the chosen parameter value to obtain its tangent components:
\[v^\mu=\left.\frac{dx^\mu(\lambda)}{d\lambda}\right|_{\lambda_0}.\]
A different chart changes the components by the chain rule. A regular change of parameter also changes their common scale, because differentiation now uses a different rate of parameter advance. In either case the tangent still describes first-order motion at one event, not a finite displacement joining separated events.
This tangent belongs to the \cref{tangent space}{math.tangent_space.definition} at \(p\). For a massive particle, choosing \cref{proper time}{sr.proper_time} as parameter gives the \cref{velocity four-vector}{sr.velocity_four_vector}. This extra choice needs a metric to define clock time. A null light path cannot use a proper-time clock parameter in the same way.
statement: A smooth worldline has a tangent at each event; its scale depends on the parameter.

title: Timelike and null cases
body:
A smooth curve alone does not say whether it can represent a material particle or light ray. Once a Lorentzian metric \(g\) is supplied, we can classify it using its nonzero tangent \(v\). With mostly-minus signature, \(g(v,v)>0\) is timelike and \(g(v,v)=0\) is null. Reversing the metric signature reverses the timelike sign but leaves the null condition unchanged.
With this additional geometric structure, material particles and physical clocks have timelike histories, while light in vacuum has null histories. Spacelike curves can occur in diagrams but do not describe material objects or signals. So this is a further application of metric geometry, rather than information supplied by a smooth manifold or chart alone.
statement: A metric distinguishes timelike material histories from null light paths.

title: Local tangent directions
body:
The plane attached at \(p\) pictures the local vector space \(T_pM\). Since the surface is two-dimensional, this space has two independent directions, even though we draw it in three dimensions.
It does not replace the terrain by a flat surface. The board agrees with the tangent plane at its own reference point; another ground point has its own tangent space. The surrounding three-dimensional picture helps visualisation, but is not part of the abstract definition.
statement: On a two-dimensional surface, \(T_pM\) is a two-dimensional space of local directions.

title: Possible directions at one point
body:
On a curved manifold, we cannot place every arrow into one preferred global vector space. Instead, each point \(p\) has its own tangent space \(T_pM\): a vector space describing possible instantaneous motion through that point.
This captures what velocities, directional derivatives and tangents to \cref{Worldlines}{math.worldline} have in common. Two routes can cross at the same point with the same first-order motion, then bend apart later. Their shared tangent keeps the instantaneous information and leaves out those later differences.
At another point there is another tangent space. Having coordinates and vectors at both points does not, on its own, tell us how to compare those vectors. A transport rule supplies that further structure.
statement: Instantaneous motion is a local vector, even when its full route curves.

title: Vectors based at one point
body:
The tangent space \(T_pM\) is the vector space of tangent vectors based at one point \(p\). Its dimension equals the manifold's local dimension: on a two-dimensional surface, there are two independent tangent directions.
Coordinates provide a convenient basis, written \(\partial/\partial x^\mu|_p\). The vertical bar reminds us that the basis is evaluated at \(p\). Changing the coordinates changes this basis and the vector's components, but not the tangent space or the vector being described.
statement: The \(n\)-dimensional vector space \(T_pM\) contains tangent vectors based at one point \(p\).

title: From curves to tangent vectors
body:
Choose smooth curves \(\gamma\) through the same point \(p\), with \(\gamma(0)=p\). In a chart \(x^i\), compare their derivatives \(v^i=dx^i/dt|_0\). Treat two curves as equivalent when all these first derivatives agree at the crossing. They then represent the same instantaneous motion, even if their later paths differ. The parameter scale is part of this comparison.
For a \cref{coordinate-transition Jacobian}{math.coordinate_transformation.jacobian} \(y^a=y^a(x)\), the chain rule gives
\[\left.\frac{dy^a}{dt}\right|_0
 =\left.\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}\right|_p v^i.\]
The Jacobian multiplies both component lists by the same invertible matrix. So if they agree in one chart, they agree in the other—and invertibility gives the converse. Each equivalence class of curves therefore defines a tangent vector independently of our coordinate choice.
To give these classes a vector-space structure, add and scale their component lists at \(p\). Every chart change uses the same linear Jacobian at this point, so transforming a component sum gives the sum of the transformed components. The operations therefore agree between charts. This constructs the coordinate-independent, \(n\)-dimensional vector space \(T_pM\).
\explanation{equivalence}{Which curves have the same tangent?}{Two curves can have equal first derivatives at \(p\) and different second derivatives. They then represent the same tangent vector but can bend apart immediately afterwards. This is why we compare first derivatives: the tangent records motion at the crossing, not the later bending of the route.}
statement: Curves with the same first-order motion at a point represent the same tangent vector.

title: Tangent vectors as directional derivatives
body:
A tangent vector can be understood by what it does to smooth scalar functions. Routes with the same first-order motion through \(p\) give the same instantaneous readout on every smooth scalar field, even if they bend differently later. So to predict the instantaneous readout, we need the tangent at the crossing, rather than the probe's whole future path.
The parameter fixes the vector's scale: if \(t\) counts seconds, \(v\) is a velocity and \(v[f]\) is a change per second. No unit length or metric has been assumed.
Let \(p=\gamma(0)\), \(v=\dot\gamma(0)\) and \(f\) be a smooth scalar field. We can express that idea by defining
\[v[f]\coloneqq\left.\frac{d}{dt}f(\gamma(t))\right|_0.\]
For local labels \(x^1,x^2\) on the two-dimensional terrain, the ordinary chain rule turns this definition into a familiar component calculation:
\[\begin{aligned}
v[f]&=v^1\partial_1f+v^2\partial_2f,\\
v^i&=\frac{dx^i}{dt},\qquad i=1,2.
\end{aligned}\]
Here \(\partial_i\) means differentiation with respect to \(x^i\). The chart gives us the partial derivatives and velocity components needed to calculate the readout. A different chart changes those ingredients together, so it does not change the motion or the resulting scalar rate.
statement: A tangent vector assigns each smooth scalar its directional rate of change.

title: Walking on a curved surface
body:
Imagine standing at a point on a sphere and considering the directions in which you could start walking. Every possible instantaneous walking velocity lies in the plane tangent to the sphere at that point. A longer route will curve over the sphere, but its initial direction still belongs to that plane.
This makes the tangent space easy to picture. It is an aid rather than a requirement: an abstract manifold still has tangent spaces even if we do not draw it inside a larger flat space.
statement: A tangent plane describes instantaneous directions, not a flat replacement for the surface.

title: Terrain survey: growth and motion
body:
At a ground point \(p\), the probe's velocity and the surface grass-growth vector \(G_p\) both belong to \(T_pM\). The terrain has two dimensions, so this tangent space has two independent directions. The two vectors describe different physical things, but use the same local vector space.
The scientist's board pictures a tangent plane at its reference point only. Elsewhere in the patch, the coordinate basis follows the coordinate curves on the ground at that location; it is not literally the same pair of arrows fixed to the flat board. This is why the board remains a labelling device rather than one tangent space for the whole patch.
statement: Grass growth and probe velocity at one ground point belong to the same tangent space.

title: Velocity is local
body:
At an event \(p\) on a particle's worldline, the curve's tangent describes its instantaneous spacetime motion. At a later event \(q\), the corresponding tangent belongs to another space, \(T_qM\).
It is tempting to subtract the two component lists and call the result a change of velocity. On a curved manifold, however, we first need a specified way to compare vectors at different points. A connection or transport rule supplies that identification. The fact that both lists have the same number of components is not enough.
statement: Comparing vectors at different points requires a specified identification or transport rule.

title: Basis and components
body:
For a chart \(x^i\) on an \(n\)-manifold, write \(\partial_i|_p\coloneqq\partial/\partial x^i|_p\). These basis vectors act on smooth scalar functions by taking the corresponding partial derivatives. A tangent vector has the expansion
\[v=v^i\partial_i|_p,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\]
with the repeated index summed.
Now change the labels to \(y^a\). The chain rule expresses a new basis derivative in terms of the old ones, using the inverse Jacobian:
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial y^a}\bigg|_p
 =\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}\bigg|_p\partial_i|_p.\]
The vector components use the forward Jacobian, as established by the \cref{coordinate-rate transformation}{math.coordinate_transformation.jacobian}. Since the forward and inverse matrices undo one another, substituting both rules into \(v=v_y^a\partial/\partial y^a|_p\) cancels the inverse factors, leaving the same vector.
This explains why a component tuple alone is incomplete: the basis tells us what those numbers multiply. On an oblique or differently scaled coordinate grid, the components are not automatically physical lengths along perpendicular unit axes.
statement: Components and basis vectors change oppositely so their combined tangent vector stays fixed.

title: Coordinate units and tangent components
body:
Keep the curve parameter fixed when comparing components. If the probe's parameter is time in seconds, then \(v^x=dx/dt\) is a coordinate rate. A rate reported as \(0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\) on a metre-labelled grid is \(50\,\mathrm{cm/s}\) on the corresponding centimetre-labelled grid. The larger numerical rate only reflects the smaller coordinate unit; the probe's motion has not changed.

Writing the numerical coordinate readings as \(x'=100x\), the chain rule gives \[v^{x'}=100v^x,\qquad \partial_{x'}=\frac1{100}\partial_x.\] The rate gains a factor of 100 while the basis derivative loses that factor, so they cancel in \(v=v^x\partial_x+v^y\partial_y\). Thus it is the combination of components and basis that represents the motion. On the surveyors' arbitrarily scaled or oblique grids, a coordinate rate is not by itself a measured speed: a metric is needed to turn the whole tangent vector into a physical speed. Coordinate independence and a choice of physical measuring rule are different issues.
statement: Changing coordinate units changes velocity components, not the motion they describe.

title: Infinitesimal is not finite
body:
A tangent vector describes first-order motion at one point. It should not automatically be read as an arrow connecting that point to a distant manifold point, because such a finite separation contains more than local directional information.
To associate a separated point with a tangent vector, we need further choices, such as a coordinate construction or a geodesic map. Those choices need not give a unique result. The local tangent construction itself makes no such global identification.
statement: A tangent vector describes first-order motion at one point, not a finite separation.

title: Linear questions about directions
body:
A \cref{tangent vector}{math.tangent_space.definition} describes a possible instantaneous motion. A covector supplies a linear readout of that vector: give it a motion, and it returns one number.
The temperature probe on the curved two-dimensional terrain makes the distinction useful. Its direction and rate of motion form a tangent velocity. The temperature field then tells us how quickly the probe warms or cools along that velocity. Motion and the rule measuring its temperature effect have different mathematical roles, even though they work together.
statement: A covector is a linear readout of a tangent vector at one point.

title: A direction asks a temperature question
body:
The smooth, time-independent temperature field gives a reading \(T(p)\) at each ground point. Motion along an isotherm gives zero instantaneous temperature change; another direction can warm or cool the probe. Let its route be \(\gamma(t)\), with \(t\) in seconds, and its tangent velocity at \(p=\gamma(0)\) be \(v\).
The \cref{directional-derivative interpretation of a tangent vector}{math.tangent_space.directional_derivative} tells us how to read the temperature rate:
\[v[T]\coloneqq\left.\frac{d}{dt}T(\gamma(t))\right|_0.\]
This readout depends on the first-order motion at \(p\), not on the probe's later route.
We now give the temperature-dependent readout a name. Define the differential at \(p\) by
\[dT_p(v)\coloneqq v[T].\]
At a fixed point, this rule is linear in \(v\): adding or scaling velocities adds or scales the readouts. That makes it a covector on \(T_pM\). Collect all the linear readout rules at the point, and we obtain the cotangent space \(T_p^*M\).
\explanation{linearity}{Why is the readout linear?}{Tangent vectors act as directional-derivative operators. Their linear combinations act on a scalar field by
\[(a v+b w)[T]=a\,v[T]+b\,w[T].\]
Thus the definition gives
\[dT_p(a v+b w)=a\,dT_p(v)+b\,dT_p(w).\]
Here \(a,b\) are numerical weights used to combine the tangent vectors. This is linearity in the tangent vector at one point, not a claim that temperature is a linear function throughout the patch.
\explanation{first-order}{Why is linearity at one point enough?}{A differential retains a smooth function's first-order change at that point. A finite journey can involve higher-order changes in temperature. Those do not alter the first-order linear rule at the starting point; they tell us when that local rule alone is insufficient for the whole journey. Different points generally have different differentials.}}
For any smooth scalar field \(f\), the same construction gives \(df_p(v)\coloneqq v[f]\). This provides an important class of covectors, but does not say that every covector field over a region comes from one scalar field. A temperature field changing with time would also contribute a change at a fixed ground point; that case is outside this example.
statement: The temperature differential turns a tangent velocity into an instantaneous temperature rate.

title: The readout on a board's grid
body:
Given the temperature differential as a linear readout, we now want a way to calculate it. Choose local coordinates \(x^1,x^2\). The probe visits the same ground points regardless of their labels.
Write \(\partial_i\coloneqq\partial/\partial x^i|_p\) for the coordinate basis vectors. Here \(i,j\) range over 1 and 2; a repeated upper/lower index is summed. We need corresponding readout rules that pick out the vector components. Define the dual covectors \(dx^i\) by
\[\begin{aligned}
dx^i(\partial_j)&\coloneqq\delta^i{}_j,\\
dx^i(v)&=v^i.
\end{aligned}\]
The Kronecker delta is one for matching indices and zero otherwise. So each basis covector reads one coordinate component, without measuring a Euclidean length. At \(p\),
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p&=(\partial_iT)_p\,dx^i,\\
v&=v^i\partial_i,\\
dT_p(v)&=(\partial_iT)_p\,v^i.
\end{aligned}\]
Applying the differential to the vector combines their expansions, giving the last line. This is the familiar chain-rule temperature rate \(dT(\gamma(t))/dt\), evaluated at the point being crossed.
\explanation{algebra}{Where does the component sum come from?}{Apply the covector to the vector, using linearity and the dual-basis rule:
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p(v)&=(\partial_iT)_p\,dx^i(v^j\partial_j)\\
&=(\partial_iT)_p\,v^j\delta^i{}_j\\
&=(\partial_iT)_p\,v^i.
\end{aligned}\]
The Kronecker delta selects matching components. The sum comes from linearity and duality alone. We have not used a dot product or chosen a metric.}
More generally, \(\omega=\omega_i dx^i\) is the coordinate expansion of a covector. The dual-basis normalisation is dimensionless, but the coefficients can carry physical units. Their pairing therefore need not be dimensionless.
statement: The dual basis reads vector components: \(dx^i(v)=v^i\), giving \(\omega(v)=\omega_i v^i\).

title: A measurement scientists can compare
body:
Suppose the local temperature derivatives are \(\partial_1T=2\,\mathrm{K/m}\) and \(\partial_2T=-1\,\mathrm{K/m}\). The probe has coordinate rates \(v^1=0.5\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and \(v^2=0.2\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Use the \cref{dual-basis component rule}{math.cotangent_space.basis} to multiply each temperature derivative by the matching coordinate rate and add the contributions:
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p(v)&=(2)(0.5)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&\quad{}-(1)(0.2)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&=0.8\,\mathrm{K/s}.
\end{aligned}\]
The positive total means that the probe is warming: the first contribution outweighs the cooling contribution from the second direction. These are coordinate rates: on an arbitrarily scaled or oblique grid, their Euclidean component length is not automatically the probe's measured physical speed.
\explanation{centimetres}{Why does a centimetre grid give the same answer?}{Relabel both coordinates from metres to centimetres. The numerical coordinate labels become 100 times larger. The probe's rates become \(50\) and \(20\,\mathrm{cm/s}\), while the temperature derivatives become \(0.02\) and \(-0.01\,\mathrm{K/cm}\). Hence
\[\begin{aligned}
dT_p(v)&=(0.02)(50)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&\quad{}-(0.01)(20)\,\mathrm{K/s}\\
&=0.8\,\mathrm{K/s}.
\end{aligned}\]
The coordinate rates increased by a factor of 100 while the derivatives decreased by that factor. They compensate because both calculations describe the same motion through the same temperature field. Coordinate independence does not mean dimensionlessness: the answer still has units K/s. The instantaneous rate is exact. Multiplying it by a finite travel time gives an exact change only if the rate stays constant; otherwise that use is an approximation.}
Think of \(dT_p\) as a readout attached to this point: give it a tangent velocity and it returns that velocity's temperature rate. It acts on tangent arrows, but does not need to be drawn as another arrow itself.
Notice that no metric was needed to obtain this temperature readout. Asking for the direction of greatest temperature increase at a fixed physical speed would require a metric to define that speed.
The same rule applies to grass growth: \(dT_p(G_p)\) is positive towards warmer ground, negative towards colder ground, and zero along an isotherm to first order.
statement: The probe warms at \(0.8\,\mathrm{K/s}\), regardless of the coordinate units.

title: The dual space of tangent vectors
body:
The cotangent space \(T_p^*M\) consists of all linear maps from the \cref{tangent space}{math.tangent_space.definition} at \(p\) to the real numbers. Its elements are called covectors or one-forms:
\[\omega:T_pM\rightarrow\mathbb R.\]
Linearity means that \(\omega(av+bw)=a\omega(v)+b\omega(w)\): combining the input vectors combines the readings in the same way.
The number \(\omega(v)\), also written \(\omega_\mu v^\mu\), is their natural pairing. It needs no metric, because the covector already is a rule for taking a vector to a scalar. We do not first need to turn either object into an ordinary Euclidean arrow.
statement: The cotangent space is the dual \(T_p^*M=\mathrm{Hom}(T_pM,\mathbb R)\) of the tangent space.

title: Covectors as linear readouts
body:
Think of a covector as a linear measuring instruction attached at \(p\). It might ask for one coordinate component of a direction, or for the instantaneous change of a scalar as we move along that direction.
Different tangent vectors can give the same reading. For example, all directions tangent to a temperature contour give zero first-order temperature change. The set of vectors receiving zero is called the covector's kernel. So the covector is a rule for sorting directions by their readout, rather than necessarily being another direction arrow.
statement: A covector measures a direction linearly; many different directions can give the same result.

title: A scalar need not be dimensionless
body:
A coordinate-independent scalar can still carry physical units. Those units depend on which covector and tangent vector we pair. For the temperature field, \(\partial T/\partial x\) has units of kelvin per coordinate unit. Pairing \(dT\) with a small displacement gives a first-order temperature change in kelvin: the coordinate unit in the derivative cancels the displacement unit. Pairing it with the probe velocity gives a temperature-change rate in kelvin per second.

No metric enters either pairing. The coordinate descriptions compensate, but there is no requirement that every physical unit cancel too. A dimensionless phase change is a different example: a phase differential paired with a displacement can be dimensionless.
statement: Coordinate-independent scalar readouts can still carry physical units.

title: The same temperature change on two grids
body:
At a terrain point suppose \(\partial T/\partial x=2\,\mathrm{K/m}\). Keep \(y\) fixed and consider \(\delta x=0.5\,\mathrm m\) within the local linear approximation. The differential predicts \[dT_p(\delta x\,\partial_x)=(2\,\mathrm{K/m})(0.5\,\mathrm m)=1\,\mathrm K.\] On a centimetre-labelled grid the same calculation is \((0.02\,\mathrm{K/cm})(50\,\mathrm{cm})=1\,\mathrm K\). The two descriptions give the same kelvin change because the covector component decreases numerically by 100 while the displacement component increases by 100.

The distinction between a differential and a finite change matters here. The differential gives an exact linear readout at \(p\), but treating that value as the actual finite temperature change is a first-order approximation. If temperature varies nonlinearly over the displacement, the approximation needs refinement.
statement: Metre and centimetre components predict the same first-order temperature change.

title: A directional-change calculation
body:
Use dimensionless coordinates and a dimensionless scalar, so that we can focus on the algebra. Let \(f(x,y)=x^2+3y\). Its partial derivatives are \(\partial_x f=2x\) and \(\partial_y f=3\), so at \(p=(2,1)\) the differential is
\[df=4\,dx+3\,dy.\]
Now give it a tangent vector with components \(v=(1,-2)\). The basis covectors read those two components, giving
\[df(v)=4(1)+3(-2)=-2.\]
The negative answer means that the scalar decreases along this instantaneous motion. We have used a covector to turn two directional components into one scalar rate, without introducing a metric.
statement: For \(f=x^2+3y\) at \((2,1)\), the direction \((1,-2)\) gives \(df(v)=-2\).

title: Contours and zero change
body:
On a contour map, moving tangent to a height contour gives no first-order change in height. The height differential therefore returns zero on that tangent direction. A direction crossing the contours can instead give a positive or negative readout.
This picture often tempts us to call the differential a perpendicular arrow. Perpendicularity needs a metric, however: the metric converts the differential into a gradient vector. Before making that extra choice, the covector is the linear rule assigning rates to directions.
statement: A scalar differential vanishes on directions tangent to its level curves.

title: Why covectors appear in physics
body:
For a wave phase \(\phi\), the covector \(d\phi\) measures phase change along a spacetime direction. Giving it different tangent vectors asks different directional phase-change questions.
In mechanics, a momentum one-form similarly pairs with an infinitesimal displacement or velocity to supply a scalar contribution to work or action. These examples explain why lower-index objects appear naturally: their role is to read vectors, rather than merely to give an alternative spelling of the same vector components.
statement: Phase differentials and momentum one-forms turn directions into scalar readouts.

title: Do not assume the metric too soon
body:
Tangent vectors and covectors have different roles before any metric is chosen: one supplies a direction, the other a linear readout of directions.
A nondegenerate metric adds a map between them, described as lowering or raising an index. Familiar Euclidean pictures often use that map without saying so, particularly when drawing a gradient as a perpendicular arrow. This is a useful identification once the metric is specified, but the cotangent space and its natural pairing do not depend on it.
statement: A metric can identify vectors with covectors, but the dual space exists without one.

title: Tensors varying over spacetime
body:
GR describes geometry and matter using quantities attached to spacetime events. Scalars, vectors and covectors are the first examples. Tensors extend that idea to quantities with several inputs or indices, while retaining a coordinate-independent meaning.
The useful starting question is what a tensor does at one point. Once we understand its inputs and scalar readout there, a tensor field lets that same kind of object vary smoothly throughout a region. This separates the tensor's local role from the way its values change from point to point.
statement: A tensor field gives a coordinate-independent geometric object at every point.

title: A smooth field of multilinear objects
body:
Let \(M\) be a smooth manifold. At a point \(p\), a tensor of type \((r,s)\) is a real-valued multilinear map with \(r\) cotangent-vector inputs and \(s\) tangent-vector inputs. Multilinear means linear in each input when the others are held fixed: scaling or adding that input scales or adds its contribution to the readout.
A tensor field assigns one tensor of the same type smoothly to every point of a region. Choosing a smooth local basis gives smooth component functions that we can calculate with. Another basis generally gives different components, but describes the same underlying tensor field.
A scalar field has type \((0,0)\). A vector is a type-\((1,0)\) tensor: give it a covector, and it returns their natural pairing. A covector is a type-\((0,1)\) tensor acting on a vector.
\explanation{point}{Must the input vectors be at the same point?}{Yes. A tensor at \(p\) acts on tangent vectors in \(T_pM\) and covectors in \(T_p^*M\). Inputs from different points belong to different spaces. To compare or transport them, we need additional structure; supplying a tensor at each point does not itself provide a transport rule.}
statement: A tensor field assigns a fixed-type tensor smoothly to each point of a manifold.

title: Point-by-point objects
body:
At a terrain point \(p\), temperature \(T(p)\), grass growth \(G_p\) and the temperature differential \(dT_p\) have different mathematical roles. A field supplies the appropriate object at every point, with components varying smoothly in a smooth local basis.
To combine such objects, first keep their base point fixed. Pairing \(dT_p\) with \(G_p\) gives a scalar readout at \(p\); repeating that local calculation across the terrain gives a scalar field.
\explanation{contraction}{Calculate one pointwise pairing}{Suppose \(\omega_i=(2,-1)\) and \(V^i=(3,4)\) in a two-dimensional basis. Multiply matching components and add:
\[\omega_i V^i=2(3)+(-1)(4)=2.\]
The repeated upper/lower index instructs us to sum. The numbers here are dimensionless for simplicity; physical pairings can carry units. No metric is needed for this natural pairing.}
A vector at another point lies in a different tangent space. Having fields at both points does not alone tell us how to compare or transport those vectors.
statement: Fields supply local objects; contractions combine them at the same point.

title: Scalars, vectors, and higher tensors
body:
The terrain survey already contains several tensor types: temperature is an order-zero scalar field, grass growth an order-one vector field, and the temperature differential an order-one covector field. Their roles differ, even when a particular chart lets us represent them all by numbers.
In GR, the metric \(g_{\mu
u}\) and covariant stress-energy tensor \(T_{\mu
u}\) have type \((0,2)\). Riemann curvature, written as \(R^ho{}_{\sigma\mu
u}\), has type \((1,3)\) and total order four. The many components are a basis description of one geometric object, rather than unrelated scalar fields.
With a metric we can also raise and lower indices. For example, \(T^{\mu
u}\) is a raised form of \(T_{\mu
u}\). This uses an additional metric-dependent map; it is not simply another coordinate labelling.
statement: Scalars, vectors, covectors, metrics and curvature tensors are different tensor types.

title: Not just an array of components
body:
An array becomes a tensor description only when we specify its basis and transformation behaviour. Two charts can assign different arrays to the same field, provided those arrays obey the correct rule on their overlap.
Equal array sizes or constant entries are not enough. The \cref{tensor transformation rule}{math.tensor_transformation_law.definition} tells us precisely how the descriptions must fit together. Some indexed quantities, such as the connection coefficients introduced later in GR, do not transform as tensors. Indices are useful bookkeeping, but not a guarantee of tensorial behaviour.
statement: An array represents a tensor only with a basis and the correct transformation behaviour.

title: Indices as bookkeeping
body:
Indices let us calculate with tensor components without writing every sum explicitly. The essential skills are to distinguish upper and lower slots, recognise which labels are summed, and check that the unsummed labels match on both sides of an equation.
These are practical bookkeeping rules, not a new physical law. Abstract-index notation takes the idea further by describing tensor slots without choosing a component basis, but we do not need that refinement to begin the calculations here.
statement: Indices record component slots, sums and the shape of tensor equations.

title: Component labels and abstract slots
body:
In a chosen coordinate basis for a \cref{tensor field}{math.tensor_field.definition}, \(V^i\) lists a vector's components and \(\omega_i\) lists a covector's components. It is important to read the superscript according to its role. Here it is an index, not a power: \(V^2\) means the second component here, whereas \((V^1)^2\) squares the first component.
An expression such as \(A^i{}_{j}\) has two index slots. Choosing a value for each index selects one entry of the component matrix; leaving them free describes the whole family of entries.
\explanation{abstract}{What changes in abstract-index notation?}{Abstract indices such as \(a,b\) describe the tensor's slots and contractions without choosing a numerical basis. Thus \(A^a{}_{b}\) describes a type-\((1,1)\) tensor. Component indices describe entries after a basis is chosen. Free and dummy indices occur in both notations. So abstract versus component indices should not be confused with curved versus flat space; it is a choice of how to describe the tensor.}
The calculations on this page use component indices unless explicitly stated otherwise.
statement: Component indices label basis entries; abstract indices describe tensor slots without choosing a basis.

title: Component indices
statement: An index range records dimension; index number and position record tensor type.

title: Repeated and free indices
statement: Repeated upper/lower indices are summed; free indices must match on both sides.

title: Indexed need not mean coordinate-bound
body:
Using component indices does not make an equation coordinate-bound in its physical meaning. If its ingredients are genuine tensors, their components can change together so that the same tensor equation holds in another smooth chart.
Matching free indices is a useful first check, but cannot prove that the ingredients have tensorial transformation behaviour. For that, we must also examine their transformation rules.
\explanation{raising}{Can an index simply be moved up or down?}{No. Lowering a vector index uses a metric:
\[V_\mu=g_{\mu\nu}V^\nu.\]
The free label \(\mu\) stays on both sides, while \(\nu\) is summed. Raising an index uses the inverse metric. These operations change the tensor representation through additional geometric structure; they are not just a renaming of a dummy index.}
statement: Matching indices is necessary for a tensor equation, but does not establish tensorial behaviour.

title: Components that transform correctly
body:
Two scientists can report different component tables for the same measurement on the terrain. That is expected, because components describe an object relative to a chosen basis. A basis change must be compensated by a component change.
For a vector, follow the same route in both coordinate grids and apply the chain rule. For a covector, ask that its readout of that vector stay fixed. These requirements lead to opposite transformation factors, which cancel when the objects are paired.
A tensor accepts several inputs and is linear in each separately, so its component rule collects one factor for each index. The transformation reconciles descriptions at the same point; it does not evolve the physical field or require its components to be constant.
statement: Different component arrays can describe the same tensor in different coordinate bases.

title: One Jacobian factor for every index
body:
Consider overlapping coordinates \(x^i\) and \(y^a\). The \cref{coordinate-transition Jacobian}{math.coordinate_transformation.jacobian} gives an invertible Jacobian and its inverse:
\[\begin{aligned}
J^a{}_i&\coloneqq\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i},\\
K^i{}_a&\coloneqq\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}.
\end{aligned}\]
At the same manifold point, tensor components in the \(y\) basis receive one \(J\) factor for each upper index and one \(K\) factor for each lower index. The old indices are summed to combine the original components, while the new free indices identify which transformed component we are calculating.
For example, a type-\((1,1)\) tensor obeys
\[T_y^a{}_b=J^a{}_i K^j{}_b T_x^i{}_j.\]
Here subscripts \(x,y\) identify the coordinate description, not extra tensor indices. For a nonlinear transition, the factors can change from point to point, so all factors and components in one calculation must be evaluated at the same point. We call this passive because the tensor itself is held fixed while its coordinate description changes.
statement: Every upper index receives a forward Jacobian; every lower index receives its inverse.

title: Vector and covector cases
body:
Let \(x^i\) and \(y^a\) be overlapping coordinates, with all quantities evaluated at the same point \(p\). A vector \(V\) can be represented by a curve through \(p\). Using the \cref{tangent-component construction}{math.tangent_space.curves}, apply the chain rule to that curve:
\[V_y^a=\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}V_x^i.\]
A covector \(\omega\) must give the same scalar readout on that vector in either chart. For this readout to agree for every possible input vector, the covector components must compensate for the vector's forward Jacobian. They therefore obey
\[\omega^y_a=\frac{\partial x^i}{\partial y^a}\omega^x_i.\]
The superscripts \(x,y\) on \(\omega\) name the chart, not extra indices. Each repeated upper/lower index is summed. Understanding that convention is the role of \cref{index notation}{math.index_notation.summation}.
The forward and inverse factors cancel in \(\omega^y_a V_y^a=\omega^x_i V_x^i\). The cancellation uses only the natural vector/covector pairing. We have not assumed perpendicular axes or introduced a metric.
\explanation{why-inverse}{Derive the covector rule from the pairing}{The scalar readout must agree for every vector:
\[\omega^y_a V_y^a=\omega^x_i V_x^i.\]
Substitute the vector rule. Since this must hold for every \(V_x^i\),
\[\omega^y_a\frac{\partial y^a}{\partial x^i}=\omega^x_i.\]
Multiplying by the inverse Jacobian undoes the forward factor and isolates \(\omega^y_a\), giving the displayed covector transformation. No metric entered the argument.}
statement: Vectors and covectors transform oppositely, preserving their scalar pairing.

title: One factor per index
body:
A \cref{tensor}{math.tensor_field.multilinear_construction} is multilinear in its tangent/cotangent inputs. We can use that multilinearity, together with the coordinate-transition Jacobian, to obtain one transformation factor per index.
At a point use overlapping coordinates \(x^i,y^a\). Use the \cref{coordinate-transition Jacobian}{math.coordinate_transformation.jacobian}, writing \(J^a{}_i=\partial y^a/\partial x^i\) and \(K^i{}_a=\partial x^i/\partial y^a\). The basis covectors and vectors obey
\[\begin{aligned}
dy^a&=J^a{}_i\,dx^i,\\
\partial/\partial y^b&=K^j{}_b\,\partial/\partial x^j.
\end{aligned}\]
A type-\((1,2)\) tensor accepts one covector and two vectors. To calculate a new component, feed the tensor one new covector basis element and two new vector basis elements. Substitute the three basis changes shown above. Since the tensor is linear in each input separately, we can pull out the coefficient in each slot, multiplying the three factors:
\[T_y^a{}_{bc}
 =J^a{}_i K^j{}_b K^k{}_c T_x^i{}_{jk}.\]
The old indices \(i,j,k\) are summed. The new indices \(a,b,c\) are free. Each extra slot contributes its own factor in the same way, so this argument extends to any tensor type.
For a covariant order-two tensor, such as a metric, both inputs are vectors. Consequently both factors are inverse Jacobians:
\[g^y_{ab}=K^i{}_a K^j{}_b g^x_{ij}.\]
\explanation{factors}{Why can the factors be pulled outside?}{Linearity in a single slot allows its basis-change coefficients to be pulled out while the other inputs are fixed. Apply that step once to each slot. Multiplying these independent coefficients gives the product of Jacobian factors; nothing in this step requires the original component functions to be linear in position. Multilinearity concerns the input vectors and covectors at one point.}
statement: Multilinearity supplies one transformation factor for each tensor index.

title: Not unchanged components
body:
A tensor can be independent of our coordinate choice while its component numbers change. Tensorial does not mean that each entry of its component table is invariant. Instead, the entries change by the rule for their index slots. The changed numbers compensate for the changed basis, preserving the same geometric object and scalar readouts at the point.
\explanation{cancel}{See the Jacobians cancel in a contraction}{Use \(V_y^a=J^a{}_j V_x^j\), \(\omega^y_a=K^i{}_a\omega^x_i\), and \(K^i{}_aJ^a{}_j=\delta^i{}_j\):
\[\begin{aligned}
\omega^y_a V_y^a&=\omega^x_i K^i{}_aJ^a{}_j V_x^j\\
&=\omega^x_i\delta^i{}_j V_x^j\\
&=\omega^x_j V_x^j.
\end{aligned}\]
The inverse and forward matrices have cancelled through the identity matrix. This establishes agreement at this one point; it does not say that the scalar must have equal values at different points.}
There is a further caution when differentiating component functions. Under a nonlinear chart change, the Jacobian factors also vary, so ordinary partial derivatives generally produce extra terms. GR uses a covariant derivative to correct for this; its construction is beyond this module.
statement: Coordinate independence does not mean that tensor components stay fixed.

title: Type, order and rank
statement: Tensor type \((r,s)\) counts upper and lower slots; total order is \(r+s\).

title: What a tensor measures
body:
The \cref{covector readout}{math.cotangent_space.definition} gives the simplest model: one vector goes in, and a scalar comes out. A covariant order-two tensor \(B\), of type \((0,2)\), accepts two vectors and returns a scalar:
\[B(V,W)=B_{ij}V^iW^j.\]
The new feature is that there are two inputs, and the map is linear in each one separately. If we hold \(W\) fixed, then \(B(V,W)\) a linear readout of \(V\); if we instead hold \(V\) fixed, then it a linear readout of \(W\).
\explanation{multilinear}{Why separately linear, not jointly linear?}{For fixed \(W\),
\[B(aV+bU,W)=aB(V,W)+bB(U,W).\]
But scaling both inputs multiplies the result twice: \(B(2V,2W)=4B(V,W)\). Each slot contributes a factor of two, so together they produce four. This is what separately linear means; it is not ordinary linearity in the pair treated as one input.}
More generally a tensor of type \((r,s)\), viewed as a scalar-valued multilinear map, accepts \(r\) covectors and \(s\) vectors. This explains the index positions: upper slots pair with covectors, and lower slots pair with vectors.
\explanation{vector-slot}{How can a vector be a tensor in this description?}{A vector \(V\) acts on a covector by returning \(\omega(V)\). Thus a type-\((1,0)\) tensor accepts one covector. A covector, of type \((0,1)\), accepts one vector. Both use only the natural vector/covector pairing, so neither requires a metric.}
statement: A tensor accepts vectors and covectors, returning a scalar linearly in each input separately.

title: A metric gives a two-input measurement
body:
At one point of a two-dimensional surface, a metric \(g\) is a symmetric bilinear map pairing two tangent vectors. In a local basis suppose
\[g_{ij}=\begin{pmatrix}4&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix}.\]
Take the component values to be dimensionless here, so we can focus on how the pairing works. For \(V^i=(1,2)\),
\[\begin{aligned}
g(V,V)&=4(1)^2+1(2)^2\\
&=8.
\end{aligned}\]
If we had silently treated the grid as unit orthonormal, we would have obtained \(1^2+2^2=5\). The supplied metric instead weights the first component by four, so the correct answer is eight. For a displacement with physical units, the metric pairing supplies squared length with the corresponding units.
For spacetime a Lorentzian metric supplies an interval rather than a positive squared length for every vector. Despite that change in sign structure, the metric is still a two-input bilinear tensor.
statement: For \(g_{ij}=\mathrm{diag}(4,1)\) and \(V^i=(1,2)\), the metric pairing gives \(g(V,V)=8\).

title: One grid stretched by a factor of two
body:
Use numerical coordinate labels with \(x'=2x\). At one point let \(V^x=3\) and \(\omega_x=8\). The forward Jacobian is two and the inverse is one half. Applying the vector and covector rules gives
\[\begin{aligned}
V^{x'}&=2(3)=6,\\
\omega_{x'}&=\tfrac12(8)=4.
\end{aligned}\]
The pairing is \(8(3)=24\) before relabelling and \(4(6)=24\) afterwards. The factor of two and its inverse compensate. Thus the component values change while their scalar readout stays fixed.
\explanation{two-index}{What happens to a two-index tensor?}{If the same rescaling is applied to a one-dimensional coordinate, a covariant component \(B_{xx}\) receives two inverse factors:
\[B_{x'x'}=\tfrac14 B_{xx}.\]
A mixed component \(A^x{}_{x}\) receives one factor of two and one of a half, so it stays unchanged in this particular rescaling. This cancellation belongs to this particular one-dimensional rescaling. A general basis change can mix components, so it does not make every mixed component individually invariant.}
statement: Rescaling coordinate labels changes components while preserving the scalar pairing.

title: Specifying a smooth structure
body:
Start with a Hausdorff, second-countable topological space (one in which distinct points can be separated by neighbourhoods, with a countable base of open sets) \(M\) that is locally homeomorphic to \(\mathbb R^n\). Being locally homeomorphic means that small regions can be labelled continuously, with continuous inverses. Choose such local maps \(x_\alpha:U_\alpha\to x_\alpha(U_\alpha)\) whose regions cover \(M\).
To support smooth calculus, we now require every overlap conversion \(x_\beta\circ x_\alpha^{-1}\), and its inverse, to be smooth. Include every chart smoothly compatible with this collection. The resulting maximal smooth atlas specifies the smooth structure, so that smoothness is a property of the manifold rather than one chosen map.
These are conditions on the starting space and the chosen atlas; an arbitrary space need not satisfy them. Notice also what has not been assigned: smooth coordinate structure alone gives no distance or curvature.
\explanation{compatibility}{What does an overlap condition buy?}{A scalar function is smooth when its expressions in the charts are smooth. If overlap conversions are smooth, replacing one chart by a compatible neighbour preserves this property by composition. So we may replace one chart with a compatible neighbour without changing whether the scalar is smooth. That is the compatibility calculus needs.}
statement: Compatible local charts specify smooth structure; this is starting data, not a curvature result.

title: Constructing a chart on a surface
body:
Suppose \(M\) is already a smooth two-dimensional surface. Using that surface structure, choose a smooth projection \(\pi:M\to B\) onto a flat board \(B\), and straight board coordinates \(\ell:B\to\mathbb R^2\). The derivative tells us how nearby surface directions map to changes of the two labels. If this derivative is invertible at \(p\), the inverse-function theorem supplies a small neighbourhood \(U\) on which
\[x\coloneqq(\ell\circ\pi)|_U\]
has a smooth inverse. Thus the restricted map gives labels from which the ground point can be recovered smoothly. This is the local coordinate chart we wanted.
The theorem is local: it guarantees a suitable small patch, not one map for the whole terrain. It also says nothing about preserving lengths. If the projection overlaps itself or its derivative becomes singular, shrink the patch or choose another board.
\explanation{board}{Why does a tangent board work nearby?}{For a regular embedded surface, projection onto its tangent plane has an invertible derivative at the point of tangency. Changing to another invertible straight grid on that plane only changes the labels, so it preserves this local invertibility. Away from that point, the chart's coordinate basis belongs to the ground surface, not to the physical board.}
statement: A smooth surface projection is a chart locally when its derivative is nonsingular.

title: From a history to a curve
body:
Take a spacetime manifold \(M\) and an interval \(I\) of real numbers. Associate each parameter value \(\lambda\in I\) with the event occupied by the particle, writing this map as \(\gamma(\lambda)\). To represent a smooth history, require those coordinate expressions to vary smoothly wherever a chart covers the curve.
On an overlap, apply the smooth chart transition to the coordinate functions. This gives a smooth description in the neighbouring chart, referring to the same events. So the construction fits together without making the curve depend on one coordinate system. A smooth increasing reparametrisation with a smooth inverse changes the labels along the same oriented history, rather than changing which events it contains.
We have represented the proposed history as a curve. Deciding whether it is timelike or null needs a metric, and deciding which histories nature permits needs physical laws as well.
statement: An ordered smooth history defines a map from a parameter interval into spacetime.

title: Building tensors from vectors and covectors
body:
Fix a point \(p\) and its finite-dimensional \cref{tangent space}{math.tangent_space.definition} \(T_pM\) with dual \cref{cotangent space}{math.cotangent_space.definition} \(T_p^*M\). For vectors \(V,W\in T_pM\) and covectors \(\alpha,\beta\in T_p^*M\), define
\[(\alpha\otimes\beta)(V,W)\coloneqq\alpha(V)\beta(W).\]
The \cref{covector pairing rule}{math.cotangent_space.basis} is linear in its vector input. Holding one input fixed therefore leaves a linear rule in the other, so this product is bilinear. Adding such products preserves that property.
Choose a basis \(e_i\) and its dual \(\varepsilon^i\), with \(\varepsilon^i(e_j)=\delta^i{}_j\). To see that these products are sufficient, expand a general bilinear scalar-valued map \(B\) in a basis:
\[B=B_{ij}\,\varepsilon^i\otimes\varepsilon^j,\]
where \(B_{ij}=B(e_i,e_j)\), with repeated indices summed.
For a mixed tensor, include vector factors as well: a vector acts on a covector by \(\omega\mapsto\omega(V)\). Using those vector factors together with covector factors, products and linear combinations span the finite-dimensional type-\((r,s)\) tensor space. Letting their coefficients vary smoothly in local smooth bases gives a tensor field.
This construction tells us which multilinear objects are available. It does not choose the coefficient values of a physical field; geometry or physical laws must supply them.
\explanation{basis}{Why does the bilinear expansion recover the map?}{Expand \(V=V^ie_i\) and \(W=W^je_j\). Bilinearity gives \(B(V,W)=B(e_i,e_j)V^iW^j\). Each dual basis covector reads the matching component. Thus the displayed product expansion gives the same result as \(B\) on every pair of inputs, which is why it represents the whole map.}
statement: Products of vector/covector pairings and their linear combinations construct tensors at one point.

title: Why the scalar pairing becomes a sum
body:
Given the \cref{natural covector/vector pairing}{math.cotangent_space.basis}, choose at one point a tangent basis \(e_i\) and dual covector basis \(\varepsilon^j\), so \(\varepsilon^j(e_i)=\delta^j{}_i\). Write a vector and covector as
\[V=V^ie_i,\qquad\omega=\omega_j\varepsilon^j.\]
We can now combine the two component expansions. Since the covector is linear, the scalar coefficients come outside its action, and the dual-basis rule gives
\[\begin{aligned}
\omega(V)&=\omega_j V^i\,\varepsilon^j(e_i)\\
 &=\omega_j V^i\,\delta^j{}_i\\
 &=\omega_i V^i.
\end{aligned}\]
The Kronecker delta has selected matching components, leaving one summed upper/lower pair. The repeated label is therefore an instruction to perform that sum. The name of that dummy label is irrelevant: replacing both copies of \(i\) by \(k\) changes no term.
This explains the contraction that Einstein notation abbreviates. The choice to omit the summation sign is a notation convention, rather than another mathematical assumption. More general contractions pair one vector-like and one covector-like slot of a tensor, reducing its total order by two.
No metric is required for this natural pairing. There is no need to raise an index first; doing so would be a separate operation requiring a metric.
statement: Expanding in dual bases turns a coordinate-independent pairing into an upper/lower contraction.

title: A locally chartable surface
body:
The point \(p\) lies in a small neighbourhood of a smooth surface \(M\). The curved grid illustrates local coordinate labels; it does not prescribe the lengths measured between them.
The surrounding three-dimensional drawing helps us picture the surface. An abstract manifold does not need that surrounding space: its local descriptions and their overlaps supply the coordinate structure.
statement: A curved surface can have ordinary local coordinates without a global flat grid.

title: From ground points to labels
body:
The left patch \(U\) and the right coordinate image refer to the same points. The map labelled \(\phi\) assigns their coordinate tuples, while its inverse takes a tuple back to its ground point.
The right-hand rectangle is a space of numerical labels. It is flat because we draw coordinate numbers on a plane, not because the curved ground has become physically flat.
statement: A chart and its inverse connect one local region with its coordinate image.

title: One point in two coordinate grids
body:
The red point appears in both charts with its own coordinate labels. The connecting cue identifies those two records of the same point; it is not a trajectory from one physical place to another.
The transition converts labels on an overlap. Its derivative, evaluated at the point, then tells us how vector components change there.
statement: Coordinate transitions connect two descriptions of the same point.

title: A history drawn in coordinates
body:
The blue curve joins successive events in a spacetime history. The horizontal axis is one spatial coordinate, and the vertical axis is \(ct\), where \(c\) is the speed of light.
Another chart can change the curve's appearance on the page without changing its physical history. Remember that this is a plot through time, rather than a spatial track drawn at one instant.
statement: The event dots belong to one spacetime history, shown in a particular coordinate plot.

title: Linear readouts of tangent directions
body:
The level-line motif suggests directions that receive equal readings and directions that cross the levels. It is a picture to help us think about a linear rule acting on tangent vectors.
Any gradient-like arrow in the drawing uses an auxiliary geometric picture. The covector itself need not be identified with a vector, and its definition does not require a metric.
statement: A covector assigns scalar readings to tangent vectors at one point.

title: A tensor at every point
body:
The repeated \(T\) symbols represent tensor assignments at different manifold points. Each local tensor acts on vectors and covectors at its own point, using a basis there for its component description.
Smoothness lets the local descriptions fit into a field. It does not, by itself, provide a rule for transporting inputs from one tangent space to another.
statement: A field supplies local tensors throughout a region, rather than one isolated component array.

title: One tensor and its component array
body:
The tensor symbol and the component array refer to one geometric object at a point. After choosing a basis, numerical indices select particular entries of the array.
Abstract indices instead indicate slots and contractions without selecting a numerical basis. The two notations emphasise different aspects of the description; neither changes the tensor's type or the object being represented.
statement: A chosen basis turns an abstract tensor into a component description.

title: Changing the component description
body:
The arrow labelled \(\Lambda\) summarises a change of component description. It does not deform the tensor physically.
For general overlapping charts, the factors are Jacobians or inverse Jacobians evaluated at the point. They need not be constant throughout the region. The index positions tell us which factors to use in a particular component calculation.
statement: Different component arrays can represent the same tensor after a change of coordinates.
